verses.note: Before Israel has a tabernacle, priesthood, or law code, God gives it a calendar. Worship begins with the ordering of time around what God has done, so that the year itself becomes a confession of redemption.

Worship is described with the same word as slavery, but the master has changed. The exodus is not freedom from all service but release into the service of the God who frees, which is why the ritual of remembrance is itself called avodah.
Worship is placed where God chooses to make his name known, and its goal is his coming to bless. The altar is not a way to summon God but a place where he promises to meet his people.
The feasts gather harvest and history into one act of worship. Israel's thanksgiving for grain is also a remembrance of rescue, so that the rhythm of the farming year keeps the exodus in view.

The renewed covenant ends with the ordinary details of offering: the right bread, the right timing, the best of the harvest. Faithfulness to God is expressed in small acts of worship repeated every year.

The day ends not with the removal of sin but with burnt offerings, the gift of the whole animal to God. Cleansing opens the way to renewed worship, and the priest returns to his ordinary service in his ordinary robes.
